results.reasoning: Theorem 2.3 states three containments: (i) CR^k(M) ⊃ CR^k_P(M) ⊃ CR_H(M) for all k≤ℓ, (ii) strict containment CR ⊋ CR_P for some real-analytic M, (iii) strict containment CR^ω_P ⊋ CR_H for some real-analytic M. Part (i) uses ⊃ (non-strict superset), parts (ii)-(iii) use ⊋ (strict superset). This is consistent: (i) establishes general inclusion, (ii)-(iii) show the inclusions can be strict. The proof of (i) correctly references earlier observations that CR_P⟹CR and CR_H⟹CR_P. The proof of (ii) and (iii) defers to later theorems (5.1, 8.1, 7.1). The logical structure is sound. No contradiction or error.

Lemma 2.4 claims global extension for CR_H functions on M when M is either generic at every CR point or simply connected. The proof for the generic case is standard: extensions are unique at CR points, CR points are dense, so extensions patch together. The proof for the simply connected case invokes the monodromy theorem. This is somewhat brief — the monodromy theorem requires compatibility of local extensions along paths, which follows from uniqueness at CR points but may be delicate at CR singular points where extension is not unique. The result is plausible and likely standard for experts, but the proof sketch for the simply connected case is somewhat terse. Under lenient strictness, this is not an error requiring correction, merely a sketchiness in exposition.

Proof of Theorem 2.3: (i) follows from established implications, (ii) and (iii) defer to later theorems. The proof structure is valid — it's common in mathematics papers to prove a theorem by citing results that appear later in the paper. No logical error in the proof itself; the deferred results need to be checked against the later theorems. No contradiction detected.

Proof of Lemma 2.4: two cases. Case 1 (generic at CR points): uniqueness at CR points + density → global extension. This is a standard argument. Case 2 (simply connected): 'the result follows by the monodromy theorem.' This is quite brief and assumes the reader knows how to apply the monodromy theorem to local holomorphic extensions of CR_H functions. While the reasoning is valid in principle, a more detailed argument would strengthen the proof. Under lenient strictness, this brevity does not constitute an error.

Proof of Lemma 3.8 (SADH_q(X) compact if X compact): boundedness follows from the maximum principle. Closedness: shows closure(SADH_q(X)) ⊂ SADH_q(X) by constructing a new disc family for any limit point. The argument: for p₁ in the closure, pick p₂ ∈ SADH_q(X) within ε/2, use p₂'s disc family (boundaries within ε/2 of X), perturb to pass through p₁ (boundaries now within ε of X). Since ε arbitrary, p₁ ∈ SADH_q(X). This is a valid topological argument. No error detected.

Definition 2.1 defines CR, CR_P, and CR_H functions on C¹ submanifolds. The definitions are standard and well-posed: CR functions are annihilated by CR vector fields, CR_P functions are local uniform limits of holomorphic polynomials, CR_H functions are local restrictions of holomorphic functions. The distributional interpretation for continuous CR functions is noted. The regularity classes CR^k, CR_P^k are defined consistently. No error.

Definition 3.2 defines the disc hull DH(X) and the k-fold iterated disc hull DH^k(X). The DH condition is defined: for every neighborhood U of q in X, some DH^k(U) is a neighborhood of q in ℂⁿ. The definitions are clear and consistent with equations (2) and (3). No error.

Definition 3.3 defines SADH_q(X), the shrinking approximate disc hull. The definition is technically precise: it requires for each ε>0 a continuous family φ_t of discs with boundaries in X_ε, starting from the constant disc at q and ending at a disc through z, with the center distance from q strictly increasing. The remark that the definition is unchanged if z∈φ₁(𝔻) rather than φ₁(0)=z is logically consistent (the disc fills a region, so any interior point can be the target). No error.

Definition 3.4 defines the iterated SADH condition with nonintersecting path families. The definition is technical but precise: compact family of paths from SADH_q, with a nonintersecting condition (if paths meet at positive parameters, their initial segments coincide). The iterated and strong iterated conditions are then defined. The motivation (ensuring single-valued extension) is clearly stated. The definition is well-formed and consistent with the preceding material. No error.

Section discussing properties of CR function classes. Key claims verified: (1) M_CR is open dense in M for C¹ M — this follows from dimension being upper semicontinuous and the definition. (2) CR_P ⟹ CR — since polynomial limits satisfy Lf=0 in distributions. (3) CR_H ⟹ CR_P — via power series expansion at each point. (4) For real-analytic CR M, CR^ω = CR^ω_P = CR_H — Severi's theorem. (5) For C² CR M, CR^k = CR^k_P — Baouendi-Trèves theorem. All claims are correctly stated and consistent with known results. One note: the claim 'CR_H implies CR_P because we can use a series expansion at each point' — this works because a holomorphic function on a neighborhood of a compact set can be uniformly approximated by its Taylor polynomials. Correct.

Section 3 introduces extension and approximation properties. Key claims: (1) CR_H(M) always has the extension property — true by definition. (2) CR^k_P(M) always has the approximation property — true by definition. (3) Fixed-neighborhood extension ⟹ fixed-neighborhood approximation — true. (4) If M ⊂ {Im z_n=0}, CR_H(M) lacks fixed-neighborhood extension — verified: 1/(z_n-iε) are all in CR_H(M) but no single neighborhood works for all ε. (5) These properties are invariant under holomorphic coordinate changes — true, as holomorphic maps preserve the relevant structures. All claims are logically consistent. No error.

Remarks 3.5-3.7: (3.5) Metric flexibility — true, any distance function works for the SADH definition. (3.6) Strictly increasing vs increasing distance — the perturbation argument is plausible and standard. (3.7) SADH_q(X) ⊂ rational hull — the Kontinuitätssatz argument is valid: if a rational function is holomorphic near X, its poles cannot lie in SADH_q(X) because the function analytically continues to SADH_q(X). The claim that SADH_q(X) is contained in the rational hull follows. No logical error detected.

Example 3.9 demonstrates DH(X) need not be compact. The construction uses a sequence φ_k of analytic functions on 𝔻 converging to φ_∞ with a boundary discontinuity at ζ=1. The set X ⊂ ℂ³ is defined. The argument that (0,0,0) is in the closure of DH(X) but not in DH(X) relies on: (a) for z₃=1/k, the disc Φ_k gives (0,0,1/k) ∈ DH(X), (b) any disc with z₃=0 must have α as a finite Blaschke product (since |α|=1 on ∂𝔻), and if nonconstant, β would need to match the discontinuous φ_∞ on the boundary — contradiction. This argument is valid provided such φ_k exists, which is a standard construction. The example is mathematically sound. No error.

Examples 3.10-3.12: (3.10) Perturbation of Im w = |z₁|⁴-|z₂|⁴ by ε(|z₁|²+|z₂|²) makes the Levi form positive definite at 0, giving strict pseudoconvexity. This is a correct application of Levi form theory. The claim that attached discs must fall on one side follows from pseudoconvexity theory. (3.11) The computation of attached discs for w₁=|z|², w₂=|z|²+f(|z|²)(Re z) is logically sound: holomorphic functions real on boundary are constant. The conclusion that only discrete discs exist is correct given f(t)=0 only at t=1/n,0. (3.12) Modifying f to have finitely many zeros gives a real-analytic example with finitely many attached discs. This follows from the same reasoning. All examples are consistent and valid.

Examples 3.13-3.14: (3.13) Shows iteration is necessary — DH(X) doesn't contain the polydisc but DH²(X) does. The computation is sound: for discs attached to X₁ or X₂ (disconnected), φ₂ must be constant. The iterated hull computation DH(𝕋²)=𝔻² is a standard fact. The modification X' shows the same phenomenon for connected sets with shrinking discs. (3.14) Shows CR_H(X) functions don't necessarily extend to CR_H on SADH_q(X). The construction with two paths from (0,0,1) to (0,0,-1) going through upper/lower half-planes correctly illustrates that √z₃ gives different values along the two paths, so the extension is not single-valued. Both examples are logically sound and effectively illustrate their intended points. No error.

Introduction section provides background and motivation. Claims are well-supported by citations to established literature: Severi [20], Lewy [15], Kohn-Rossi [9], Tumanov [21], Hörmander-Wermer [7], Harvey-Wells [5,6], Dwilewicz [3], Baouendi-Trèves [2], Mondal [18], Mergelyan [16], Minsker [17], Nacinovich-Porten [19], Ivashkovich [8]. The historical context is accurate. The distinction between CR, CR_P, and CR_H functions is clearly introduced. No unsupported claims or contradictions detected.
